comments.author: mannuch
comments.story: Memory safety is necessary, not sufficient
comments.why: One of a couple great talks on Swift's C++ migration story
comments.text: I wonder what the author thinks about Swift’s new C++ interop story? Since the Swift compiler includes Clang, and can thus compile both your C++ and Swift into LLVM IR, without the need for an FFI later between the two, couldn’t this be the “Typescript for C++” that the author points out a space for? The Swift folks are very much thinking about Swift as a C++ successor that can be incrementally migrated to so I’m a bit surprised the author didn’t discuss it further — especially given Swift’s spiritual similarities to Rust. There’s a couple great talks on this by folks on the Swift team. John McCall at CppNow [VIDEO] Konrad Malawski at StrangeLoop 2023 [LINK]

comments.story: Safe and efficient C++ interoperability via non-escapable types and lifetimes
comments.why: Apple wants to migrate from C++ to a safe low-overhead Swift
comments.text: Apple wants to migrate away from C++, including code in the kernel, so they need a safe, low-overhead language. Swift has originally been designed as an ObjC replacement, mostly for UI glue code, with conveniences more like a scripting language. So now they're working on making Swift support more low-level low-overhead code. [VIDEO]

comments.author: stephen_g
comments.story: Apple hiring compiler developers for improving Swift / C++ interoperability
comments.why: Presenter explains writing new C++ project features in Swift
comments.text: They definitely have opened some things up, like a full C++ interface to Metal. I think the idea with this current effort is kind of the opposite though - not to encourage more use of C++, but to start writing new features of C++ projects in Swift (the presenter at the C++ Now 2023 talk [1] goes into this). I expect WebKit is a big target for them, I think they eventually want to replace all their C++ with Swift gradually (instead of trying to do ground-up rewrites, where you dedicate a team to doing that for years and you have a replacement at the end with fewer features than the old project). 1. comments.author: nrr
comments.story: Swift was always going to be part of the OS
comments.why: Source that Apple adopts Swift as successor to C and C++
comments.text: The raisons d'être between the CLR (and C#) and Swift are entirely different. Apple has explicitly set out to adopt Swift as a successor language to C, Objective-C, C++, and Objective-C++[0][1]. This stands in stark contrast to Microsoft's vision for the CLR, which was… to be a better Java, more or less? (Does anyone actually know what the .NET initiative was all about? Microsoft went absolutely ham on it in their branding, but the momentum unceremoniously fizzled out before Server 2003 went RTM.) That said, apropos .NET fitting into Windows, the work on Singularity[2] by MSR had a lasting impact. I'm told that there is in use a System C# dialect that generates native object code via a more production grade version of Bartok[3]. 0: [VIDEO] 1: [LINK] . 2: [LINK] 3: [LINK]

comments.author: stephen_g
comments.story: Operation Triangulation: What you get when attack iPhones of researchers
comments.why: Source for Apple's plan to incrementally replace C++ with Swift
comments.text: That is exactly their plan. Swift could always link into C applications, and they have recently come out with C++ interoperability [1] so things like WebKit etc. can start having parts re-written or new parts written from the start in Swift so they can gradually replace C and C++ codebases instead of trying to rewrite everything (which sucks because even for things much, much less complex than WebKit, you can have a team working for three years working on a replacement and it’ll have less features than the original had when you started). They’re even working on an embedded subset for embedded devices so things like microcontrollers like battery management, the Secure Enclave etc. can run it. 1. [VIDEO]

comments.author: pohl
comments.story: Interoperability: Swift’s Super Power
comments.why: Supports point that interop enables gradual transition to Swift
comments.text: Don’t forget that this interoperability was put in place to support a specific engineering goal: to make it possible to slowly (over decades, probably) transition from 4 different languages (C, ObjC, C++, ObjC++) at every level of Apple’s stack towards a single successor language. Would you recommend they wait for some weird Java-esque 100% Pure implementation within the compiler itself before they can begin that work? The ideal you’re suggesting is actually made more possible by this work. One can imagine a Swift LLVM/Clang now. See: [VIDEO]

comments.author: stephen_g
comments.story: PostScript’s Sudden Death in Sonoma
comments.why: Details Apple's transition layers from C, ObjC and C++ to Swift
comments.text: Apple have chosen to go all in on Swift for their first-party code, from the kernel to the libraries to the apps. Even things running on microcontrollers (but there’s no official or standard embedded Swift subset yet). It’s quite interesting actually that they’ve very intentionally focused on building transition layers so they can start gradually integrating Swift into C, Objective-C, and recently new support for C++ and Objective-C++. See this talk for the details on that - [VIDEO] So don’t expect to see any Rust code from Apple, although of course they might ship third party things written in it at some point.
